Jonas / Vanessa —

Thanks for the walkthrough last week. As we prepare our internal security RFP response and move toward a scoped SOW, our InfoSec team asked for a short clarifying note on a few items specific to Private (VPC/on‑prem/air‑gapped) deployments. Can you confirm the following points and share any artifacts where available?

1) Network segmentation: do you provide a recommended segmentation diagram for on‑prem installs (control plane, inference pool, management/workstation, telemetry egress)? We're looking for a template we can map to our network zones.

2) Offline/air‑gapped patching: what is the supported workflow for applying OS and runtime updates when the deployment cannot reach Redwood's public endpoints? Are packages signed? How are packages transported and audited?

3) SBOM and supply chain attestations: will you provide SBOMs for the runtime and the packaged model binaries used in production? If so, in what format and cadence?

4) Emergency admin access and break‑glass: if Helix needs emergency temporary access for a P1 incident, what are the procedures, approvals, and audit trails?

5) Evidence: any short artifacts (network diagram, sample SBOM, admin‑audit sample) you can attach would help speed our internal signoff.

We'd like to lock answers by end of week to keep procurement on schedule.

Appreciate the help—
Alan Reed
VP, Infrastructure Security

Alan —

Thanks for the clear list. Short answers up front, followed by details and attachments. Attaching a recommended segmentation diagram and a small SBOM sample.

1) Network segmentation (attached: redwood-network-segmentation_v1.pdf)
   - We recommend four zones: Management (bastion/workstations), Control Plane (control services, orchestration), Inference Pool (GPU hosts, model runners), and Telemetry/Egress (log/metrics relay).
   - Control Plane can be in a restricted subnet with an allowlist for management IPs; inference hosts should be isolated from customer‑facing networks with NATed egress only to internal telemetry collectors.

2) Offline/air‑gapped patching
   - Workflow: we publish signed patch bundles (tar.gz + detached signature) to an offline delivery package. Customer pulls bundle via secure transfer (SFTP/USB handled by their operations) and runs local verification tooling (we provide a verification binary).
   - Signing: packages are signed with our code‑signing key (RSA‑4096) and an associated timestamp signature. We support verifying via customer‑provided Root CA if they require trust chaining to their HSM; otherwise our public key can be ingested into the verification tool.
   - Auditing: the verification step writes a local audit entry (admin user, timestamp, bundle hash) to the management node. We also provide an optional upload manifest that the customer can send back to Redwood for cross‑validation when connectivity is allowed.

3) SBOM and supply chain attestations (attached: sbom_redwood_runtime_2028-07.csv)
   - We provide SBOMs for the Redwood runtime and our packaging layer. SBOMs are delivered as SPDX/csv exports by default and updated with each runtime patch (typical cadence: monthly for runtime; model SBOMs on model version changes).
   - For model binaries, we provide metadata manifests (hashes, provenance: source model id, quantization step) and can arrange attestations from our model onboarding team on request. For regulated customers we sign attestations as a separate artifact.

4) Emergency admin access / break‑glass
   - Process: customer raises a break‑glass request via an agreed channel (secure ticket + signed approval from two designated Helix approvers). Once validated, Redwood support creates a time‑bound access token and performs role‑restricted session provisioning.
   - Approval & audit: all sessions are live‑recorded (console/SSH) and session transcripts stored in the management node audit store; we provide an export (admin‑access‑audit‑sample.csv) showing the schema.

5) Evidence: attached three small artifacts above. Also happy to provide a short recorded screen walkthrough of the offline verification process.

Next steps: If that covers it, Vanessa can coordinate a short recorded demo for your Ops team and Marissa (security) can share the SOC2/supply‑chain attestation references.

Would you prefer a short call tomorrow or a demo link we can record?

—

Alan / team —

I'll answer the Infosec follow ups with specifics so your auditors have concrete text they can reference in the appendix:

• Hashing and signature format
  - Hash: we compute SHA‑256 for all published bundle artifacts (tar.gz, zip, individual binaries). The verification tool checks the bundle content against the SHA‑256 manifest before signature validation.
  - Signature: we provide a PKCS#7 (CMS) detached signature (.p7s) along with each bundle and a PEM export of our signing cert chain. For customers that require HSM‑backed verification, we can supply the root certificate and signing cert metadata so you can ingest into your verification pipeline.

• Firmware updates
  - Redwood does not ship vendor firmware images. Firmware (BIOS/UEFI, vendor NIC/fw) remains customer responsibility. Our recommendation (and the sequencing we document in the playbook): apply vendor firmware + firmware microcode updates first during a maintenance window, validate hardware health, then apply Redwood runtime patch bundle. We include a pre‑flight health check in the runtime installer that verifies device drivers and kernel modules expected by the runtime.

• SBOM & attestations
  - Export formats: SPDX (JSON) and CSV are both supported; we can produce a signed PDF attestation that references the SBOM (hashes and build metadata) on request. Turnaround for a signed runtime SBOM attestation is typically 2 business days once requested.

Attached are an example SBOM (CSV) and a short admin audit sample export (admin‑access‑audit‑sample.csv) so your compliance team can inspect the schema.

Operational notes:
- Break‑glass approvals must include two named Helix approvers (we'll capture the names in the SOW and pre‑seed the approval list).
- All break‑glass sessions are restricted to a named support engineer and are limited to the minimum set of actions required; session transcripts are retained for 24 months by default (configurable).

Let me know if you want a short writeup we can drop into your controls appendix (we can provide copy‑paste text). If everything looks good, Vanessa will follow up on scheduling a recorded demo and we can kick procurement.

—
